nameStory: The fig-leaved goosefoot gets its name from its distinctive leaves that are shaped remarkably like those of a fig tree, with deep lobes and notches. The 'goosefoot' part comes from the way many plants in this family have leaves shaped like a goose's webbed foot, though this species took the resemblance in a different direction.
description: Fig-leaved goosefoot is an annual weed with uniquely shaped leaves that really do look like fig leaves in miniature. This sprawling plant grows 1-3 feet tall with branching stems and clusters of tiny, inconspicuous greenish flowers. Originally from Asia, it's become a cosmopolitan weed that pops up in disturbed soils, though it's quite rare in New England with only a couple confirmed sightings.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: The leaves are the star feature - deeply lobed with 3-5 finger-like projections that create a distinctive fig-leaf silhouette. They feel slightly mealy or dusty to the touch and have a dull, grayish-green color.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny greenish clusters appear along the stems and at branch tips, lacking petals and easily overlooked. Each flower is less than 1/8 inch across and has a powdery appearance.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms a bushy, spreading annual plant that branches from the base. The whole plant has a somewhat weedy, unkempt appearance with stems that may sprawl or stand upright.

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Produces small, dark, lens-shaped seeds that are smooth and shiny when mature. Seeds develop within tiny papery sacs that remain on the dried flower clusters.

habitat: Look for fig-leaved goosefoot in disturbed agricultural areas, waste ground, and along roadsides where soil has been turned or compacted. It prefers rich, fertile soils and can tolerate some salt, making it occasional around urban areas and farmland edges.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate in late spring when soil warms. Young plants start small with the characteristic lobed leaves already visible.
seasonality.summer: Flowers bloom throughout summer in small greenish clusters. The distinctive fig-shaped leaves are at their most prominent and easiest to identify.
seasonality.fall: Seeds ripen and plants begin to dry out, turning brownish. The dried seed clusters persist on the dead stems.
seasonality.winter: Only dried stems and seed heads remain, which may persist into early winter before breaking down completely.

funFact: This plant is considered an 'archaeophyte' - a species that was introduced to Europe so long ago (likely with early agriculture thousands of years ago) that it's become part of the traditional flora, traveling with crops and farming practices across continents.
confusionNotes: The deeply lobed leaves make this species quite distinctive from other goosefoots, but young plants might be confused with common lambsquarters until the characteristic fig-shaped leaves develop fully. Remember: if it looks like a tiny fig leaf, you've likely found your plant!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being part of the goosefoot family, this species doesn't have the typical goose-foot-shaped leaves that give the family its name - instead, it's evolved its own unique leaf shape that's unmistakable once you know what to look for.
compareHints: Unlike common lambsquarters which has simple diamond or triangular leaves, fig-leaved goosefoot has deeply divided, lobed leaves that are unmistakable. Other goosefoots in our area have relatively simple leaf shapes, making this species stand out dramatically from its relatives with its fig-like foliage.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Common lambsquarters is much more widespread than its relatives like pitseed goosefoot or fig-leaved goosefoot in New England.
Among New England goosefoots, pitseed goosefoot stands out for its strongly toothed lower leaves and honeycomb-pitted seeds.
Fogg's goosefoot is distinguished from Common Lambsquarters by having more triangular, less elongated leaves and typically being smaller overall.

Desert goosefoot stands out from other New England goosefoots primarily by its exceptionally powdery texture - much more pronounced than the light dustiness of common lambsquarters or other relatives.
Tree spinach dwarfs its goosefoot relatives like common lambsquarters, which rarely exceed 3-4 feet tall and have much thinner stems.
Unlike the common lambsquarters with its plain green leaves dusted with white powder, striped goosefoot has those unmistakable light stripes running through each leaf.
